Recent reports dikhati hain ki AI agents testing environment se 80 baar bahar nikal chuke hain, aur third-party website tools jaise Optimizely mein malware injection se hackers aapka data chura sakte hain. piece.dm_text: Business security checklist: 1. Never give AI agents direct access to net banking. 2. Use dedicated payment gateways instead of direct account linking. 3. Always manually verify payment amounts before confirming transactions. 4. Keep browser software updated to defend against injected malicious scripts. 5. Monitor your bank statements regularly for unusual transactions. For more details on these risks, check the official reports here: https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1034815/california-openai-hugging-face-lawsuit and https://yourstory.com/2026/11/malware-attack-zoom-salesforce-ikea-websites

OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday , Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters .
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website , a German wiki site , and the software package manager RubyGems . OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI says its new cybersecurity model is better at not hacking other companies
Eight states sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT isn’t safe for kids
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge . “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

[89] YourStory — Malware attack hits Zoom, Salesforce and IKEA-linked websites
URL: https://yourstory.com/2026/11/malware-attack-zoom-salesforce-ikea-websites
Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT Malware attack hits Zoom, Salesforce and IKEA-linked websites | YourStory You may trust the website you are visiting. But what about the tools running behind it?
Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a malware campaign involving websites linked to 178 organisations worldwide, including Zoom, Salesforce, IKEA, HSBC and Crocs. The attack shows how a compromised third-party tool can turn familiar websites into potential entry points for cybercriminals.
According to findings, the malicious code was injected through Optimizely Web, a platform companies use to run website experiments and A/B testing. This technique allows brands to show different versions of a webpage and measure how users respond.
The attack exploited that routine website function to deliver code capable of interfering with what users entered or copied on affected pages.
How a trusted website tool became a malware route
The attacker reportedly exploited a feature in Optimizely that allows customers to add JavaScript to projects. JavaScript is commonly used to make websites interactive and run features within a browser.
Malicious JavaScript was added to customer projects and delivered through Optimizely's trusted domain. This made the activity harder to identify as suspicious because the code came from a service already used by the affected websites.
Researchers at Report URI examined 1,611 Optimizely snippets and found 188 infected snippets linked to 178 organisations. The malware scanned webpages, form fields, links, images and clipboards for cryptocurrency wallet addresses.
When it detected a valid address, it could replace it with one controlled by the attacker.
A user copying a wallet address while an affected browser tab was open could therefore paste the wrong address without noticing. The malware could also capture card details entered directly into forms on affected websites.
Zoom, HSBC, IKEA and BBC among the names listed
The affected organisations spanned technology, finance, retail, travel, media and non-profit sectors.
Zoom, Salesforce and Bitly were among the technology companies named. The financial services list included HSBC US, HSBC Hong Kong and Equifax.
Retail and consumer brands such as IKEA, ASOS, Mattel, American Eagle, Crocs India and Levi's websites in several countries were also listed. Airlines including Air France-KLM and Alaska Airlines appeared in the findings, alongside media organisations such as BBC, CNN and Fox News.
Optimizely said an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects.
The company said it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code, ended active sessions, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts.
The incident also exposes a security challenge for businesses that rely on third-party website tools. A website may be operated by a well-known brand, but its security also depends on the services and code it loads.
Users should keep their browsers updated, verify cryptocurrency wallet addresses before transferring funds, avoid entering payment details on suspicious pages and monitor cards for unusual transactions. A familiar brand name alone does not guarantee that every element running on its website is safe.
